extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary and elementary/secondary educational institution administrators, Title IX coordinators, legal counsel, and compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for educational institutions to implement the Department of Education's final Title IX regulations, covering definitions (e.g., actual knowledge, complainant), grievance procedures, evidence access, supportive measures, recordkeeping, impartiality, and coordination with the Clery Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of actual knowledge (§106.30)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual knowledge is notice of sexual harassment or allegations of sexual harassment to a recipient's Title IX Coordinator or any official of the recipient who has authority to institute corrective measures on behalf of the recipient, or to any employee of an elementary and secondary school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In elementary and secondary schools, notice to any employee conveys actual knowledge. For postsecondary institutions, the Department gives recipients discretion to determine which employees (other than the Title IX Coordinator) have authority to institute corrective measures; notice to such officials conveys actual knowledge. Distinct from whether an employee is a Clery Act campus security authority (CSA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate indifference response standard (§106.44(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a recipient has actual knowledge of sexual harassment in its education program or activity against a person in the United States, the recipient must respond promptly in a manner that is not deliberately indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt response obligation attaches when actual knowledge exists (per §106.30). A recipient with actual knowledge must offer supportive measures and follow grievance procedures as required by the regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional designation of officials with authority to institute corrective measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Postsecondary institutions may determine which employees, other than the Title IX Coordinator, have authority to institute corrective measures on behalf of the recipient; this designation is independent of CSA status under the Clery Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may designate all CSAs or a subset as officials with authority; alternatively, institutions may keep some employees as confidential resources. Nothing prevents recipients from giving more employees authority or training more employees about reporting, but only designated officials trigger actual knowledge under Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campus Security Authorities (CSAs) vs. Title IX reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: CSAs have crime-reporting obligations under the Clery Act, which are separate from who constitutes an official with authority to institute corrective measures for Title IX purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a CSA also has authority to institute corrective measures, notice to that CSA requires the institution's prompt Title IX response regardless of whether the conduct is a Clery Act crime. If a CSA is not an official with authority for Title IX, the institution may choose whether that CSA must report sexual harassment to the Title IX Coordinator or remain a confidential resource for students and employees. CSA Clery reporting may still be required even if the CSA is designated confidential for Title IX purposes; Clery reporting does not require revealing a student's identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere ability/obligation to report or training does not confer authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere ability or obligation to report sexual harassment, to inform a student how to report, or having been trained to do so does not qualify an individual as one who has authority to institute corrective measures on behalf of the recipient under §106.30.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training or a duty to report is insufficient by itself to make an employee an 'official with authority'; recipients may, however, choose to grant authority or train more employees as they see fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal access to evidence (§106.45(b)(5)(vi))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide both parties an equal opportunity to inspect and review any evidence obtained as part of the investigation that is directly related to the allegations in a formal complaint, including evidence the recipient does not intend to rely on, and inculpatory or exculpatory evidence whether obtained from a party or other source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to completion of the investigative report, the recipient must send the evidence subject to inspection and review to each party and the party's advisor, if any, in an electronic format; parties must have at least ten days to submit a written response which the investigator will consider before completing the report. This ensures both parties can meaningfully respond to evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of evidence disclosure (directly related evidence only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence disclosure is limited to evidence that is 'directly related to the allegations raised in a formal complaint.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitive records (e.g., mental health or past victimization records) are not always directly related; parties are not required to submit such records. If a party chooses to submit sensitive records and they are directly related, the other party will have the opportunity to review and inspect them. The Department rejects an approach requiring exclusion of irrelevant or prejudicial evidence for both parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party/bystander reporting and actual knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A bystander or someone who witnesses sexual harassment may report such sexual harassment to the Title IX Coordinator or another official who has authority to institute corrective measures; when a person does so, the recipient has actual knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must respond pursuant to §106.44(a) when actual knowledge arises from third-party reporting; the regulations do not preclude responding to reports made by persons other than the person who experienced the harassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retaliation prohibition (§106.71)
rubrics_metrics.description: No recipient or other person may intimidate, threaten, coerce, or discriminate against any individual for the purpose of interfering with any right or privilege secured by Title IX or these regulations, or because the individual has made a report or complaint, testified, assisted, participated, or refused to participate in any manner in an investigation, proceeding, or hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The retaliation provision protects all persons who may be involved in a report, investigation, proceeding, or hearing under the regulations. The Department added §106.71 in response to comments emphasizing the need for anti-retaliation protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record retention period (§106.45(b)(10))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must create, make available to the complainant and respondent, and maintain records of sexual harassment investigations, results, appeals, and all training materials for a period of seven years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department revised the retention requirement from the proposed three years to seven years to align with the Clery Act's retention period for consistency and simplicity, although the periods need not be identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures: definition, nature, and obligation (§106.30 and §106.44(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures are non-disciplinary and non-punitive individualized services; examples include counseling, extensions of deadlines or other course-related adjustments, modifications of work or class schedules, campus escort services, mutual restrictions on contact, changes in work or housing locations, leaves of absence, increased security/monitoring, and other similar measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must offer supportive measures in response to a report of sexual harassment if the recipient has actual knowledge under §106.44(a), irrespective of whether a formal complaint is filed. The Title IX Coordinator must promptly contact the complainant to discuss availability, consider the complainant's wishes, inform of availability with or without filing, and explain the formal complaint process. Supportive measures must be individualized and not unreasonably burdensome to the other party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'complainant' (§106.30)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complainant is defined as 'an individual who is alleged to be the victim of conduct that could constitute sexual harassment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differs from Clery Act terminology ('victim') and aligns with Title IX's purpose to address sex discrimination. Under the final regulations, a recipient has an obligation to respond to a report of sexual harassment irrespective of whether the complainant files a formal complaint; the Department removed language that limited complainant status to persons on whose behalf the Title IX Coordinator filed a formal complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality, conflicts of interest, and bias standard (§106.45(b)(1)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals designated as Title IX Coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, or facilitators of informal resolution must not have a conflict of interest or bias for or against complainants or respondents generally, or an individual complainant or respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must train Title IX personnel to serve impartially, avoid prejudging facts, and use materials free from reliance on sex stereotypes. The Department declines to further define 'conflict of interest' or 'bias' in the regulations, leaving recipients discretion to determine what constitutes a conflict in context, though the regulations specify certain role separations (see dual roles prohibition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions on dual roles in grievance process
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision-maker who makes a written determination regarding responsibility cannot be the same person as the Title IX Coordinator or the investigator; the decision-maker for an appeal cannot be the Title IX Coordinator or any investigator or decision-maker who reached the original determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These role separations are intended to reduce structural conflicts and preserve impartiality. Recipients retain some discretion in staffing but must comply with the prohibitions stated in §106.45(b)(7) and §106.45(b)(8)(iii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trauma-informed training permitted if consistent with impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may train Title IX personnel in trauma-informed approaches or practices so long as training and practices are consistent with §106.45(b)(1)(iii) (i.e., serve impartially, avoid prejudging, and use materials free from sex stereotypes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trauma-informed practices are allowable but must not create bias or conflict with the requirement that personnel remain impartial and avoid sex-stereotyped materials; annual trainings required by Clery do not conflict with Title IX provided impartiality standards are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal resolution/mediation requirements (§106.45(b)(9)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal resolution processes (including mediation) are permitted only if both parties provide voluntary, written consent to participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most mediations do not require a standard of evidence or formal investigation; the Department's Office of Postsecondary Education may provide technical assistance on whether mediation constitutes a disciplinary proceeding under Clery Act requirements. Recipients must ensure informal resolution meets Title IX requirements and that both parties consent in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination and differences with the Clery Act
rubrics_metrics.description: The Title IX regulations do not implement or revise the Clery Act; the two regimes have different purposes and definitions (e.g., Clery uses 'victim' and defines Clery crimes), and obligations under the Clery Act differ from Title IX obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department may align certain provisions for consistency (e.g., seven-year record retention) but does not adopt Clery Act terminology wholesale. Recipients should not assume identical rules apply; for example, conduct may be a Clery crime but not meet the Title IX definition of sexual harassment, and vice versa. Creating a unified 'Clery/Title IX reporting list' could conflate distinct regulatory obligations and sow confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary and secondary school notice rule
rubrics_metrics.description: In elementary and secondary school contexts, notice to any employee of the school conveys actual knowledge to the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differs from the postsecondary approach where recipients may designate which employees have authority to institute corrective measures. Title IX obligations in the K-12 context are therefore broader with respect to who receives notice that triggers a required response.
